did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 148 is structured as a broad call to praise: first to the heavens and the heavenly realms, then to the earth and nature, and finally to all human beings.
Did you know? Among the first called to praise are the angels and “all his host”—a phrase referring to the heavenly army and celestial powers.
Did you know? The sun, moon, and stars are described in the psalm as part of all creation joining in the praise of the Lord.
Did you know? Alongside the heavenly bodies, the psalm also mentions the “highest heavens” and the waters above the heavens, thus describing the full expanse of the heavens in biblical language.
Did you know? The reason for the praise is stated explicitly: the Lord commanded, and they were created. Creation itself is the basis for the call to praise.
Did you know? According to the psalm, the Lord established the created things forever and ever and gave them a law that will not pass away; this emphasizes the order and permanence of creation.
Did you know? The call to praise descends from the heavens to the earth and includes the sea creatures and the depths—the forces and depths of the watery world.
Did you know? The psalm lists many natural phenomena—fire, hail, snow, vapor, and stormy wind—and calls them all agents that carry out the Lord’s word.
Did you know? The animal kingdom appears in a broad, graduated list: wild animals and livestock, crawling creatures and birds, alongside the mountains, trees, and cedars mentioned earlier.
Did you know? The call to praise includes all human society: kings, nations, princes, and judges, followed by young men, young women, old and young—people of every status and age.
